newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Moslem Philippines holds sedate, peaceful polls.
newsitem.headline: Moslem Philippines holds sedate, peaceful polls.

text.p: Thousands of Moslem rebels swapped their guns for ballots on Monday and voted to elect their chief as regional governor in what officials called "boringly peaceful" elections in the southern Philippines.

In a country where passions flare and dozens normally die in election fights, officials reported no major violence in any of the four Moslem provinces comprising a semi-autonomous Moslem region that Nur Misuari is to rule for the next three years.
But there was one casualty. A 79-year-old woman collapsed in the heat and died of a heart attack after voting in Maguindanao province, the election commission said.

Misuari, a former university professor who plunged the Mindanao region into 24 years of bloody civil war, cast his vote in a schoolhouse in his home town in Jolo and said it signalled his warriors' return to the political mainstream.
"This vote symbolises our commitment to peace, democracy and progress for our people here in Mindanao and eventually for the entire country," he said.
The chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) signed a peace deal with the government last week, ending the long separatist war that killed more than 120,000 people.
Christians fiercely oppose the deal and accuse Manila of selling out.
Misuari ran unopposed and needed just one vote -- his or that of one of his two wives -- to win the governorship of a region considered to be among the poorest in the country.
He is expected to be proclaimed the winner on Wednesday after the official count.
"The elections were very boring," poll commissioner Regalado Maambomg told reporters. "Boringly peaceful," said fellow commissioner Remedios Fernando.

Official poll watchers reported cases of cheating in Lanao del Sur province, where armed partisans of candidates vying for seats in a 21-member regional assembly fired their guns in the air forcing officials to cancel voting in 55 precincts, two percent of the total of 2,688.
More than 2,000 rebels, many wearing battle fatigues but without their guns, voted in Maguindanao in the first hours of polling. Thousands more cast their votes in the other areas.
President Fidel Ramos said he expected Mindanao's economy to now take off.
"The era of peace that Mindanao will now enjoy offers a unique opportunity for the region...to emerge from the economic backwaters to the front door of progress," Ramos said in Manila.
Under his peace deal with Manila, Misuari will also head a presidential council to supervise the development of 14 provinces.
The council will serve as the precursor of a much wider autonomous regional government covering provinces that will vote to join it in a plebiscite.

Many Christians fear the deal could lead to MNLF political ascendancy in Mindanao, which Moslems regard as their ancestral homeland but which Christian settlers now dominate by a ratio of three to one.
